title: Early and delayed puberty in boys and girls: when to see a doctor
behavior_type: توقيت البلوغ — المبكر والمتأخر ومتى يُراجَع الطبيب
reference_info: NHS: Early or delayed puberty · Starting your periods · الأكاديمية الأمريكية لطب الأطفال (HealthyChildren.org): Precocious Puberty · Delayed Puberty in Boys · Physical Changes During Puberty — اطّلعنا عليها في 5 أكتوبر 2026
text_original: This unit draws on public health guidance pages accessed on 5 October 2026. We restated their facts in our own words rather than quoting their text: (1) NHS, “Early or delayed puberty”: it is normal for puberty to begin at any time between 8 and 14; signs before 8 may mean early puberty, and not starting by 15 may mean delayed puberty; it is usually no cause for concern, but see a doctor if this is suspected, as investigations may identify a cause; investigations include blood tests for hormone levels, a wrist X-ray to help estimate expected height, and sometimes ultrasound or MRI; treatment is usually needed only if there are physical or psychological problems; it may run in families; causes include problems with the ovaries, testicles or hormones, illnesses such as cystic fibrosis and diabetes, and malnutrition. (2) AAP, “Precocious Puberty”: early puberty starts before 8 in girls and before 9 in boys; signs in girls include progressive breast development, faster height growth and early periods; signs in boys include enlargement of the penis and testicles, increased muscle and body hair, faster height growth and a deeper voice; it is usually an acceleration of the normal process, sometimes caused by a problem in the pituitary gland or brain, and rarely in the ovaries or testicles; the adrenal glands may release weak hormones, causing pubic or underarm hair and body odor before 8, which usually needs no treatment; exposure to creams, medicines or supplements containing hormones can cause early puberty; diagnosis includes reviewing the growth chart and a physical examination, blood tests for hormones, a hand and wrist X-ray to determine “bone age”, and sometimes a brain MRI. (3) AAP, “Delayed Puberty in Boys”: 95% of boys start puberty between 9 and 14, so it is considered delayed if it has not begun by 14; testicular enlargement is the first sign; the most common cause is constitutional delay in healthy boys who eventually enter puberty, inherited from one or both parents in about two-thirds of cases; chronic illnesses may delay it; most are shorter than peers and usually catch up by 18 with normal height; investigations include hormone blood tests and hand and wrist X-rays; treatment is usually waiting and reassurance, though an endocrinologist may offer a short course of treatment. (4) AAP, “Physical Changes During Puberty”: the first sign in girls is breast development at about 10, though it may start at 8 or as late as 13; examine a girl if puberty starts before 8 and consult a doctor if no sign has appeared by 13; examine a boy if it starts before 9 and consult a doctor if no sign has appeared by 14; if a child seems much shorter or taller than peers, speak to the pediatrician. (5) NHS, “Starting your periods”: see a doctor if periods have not started by 15, or by 13 if there are no other signs of puberty; causes of delay include low weight, excessive exercise, stress and hormone disturbances. (6) AAP, “Physical Development: What's Normal? What's Not?”: timing is largely determined by what is inherited from parents; small differences from peers are rarely concerning, while large differences warrant talking to a pediatrician. (7) ramadan_family.json, “Fasting ladder”: “The details of the signs of puberty should be sought from scholars.”
text_simplified:
When is puberty considered early or delayed? Puberty usually begins between 8 and 13 in girls and between 9 and 14 in boys, according to the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP). Timing varies widely between children and is largely determined by what they inherit from their parents. It is usually no cause for concern, but a doctor checks for an underlying cause.

Early puberty: signs before 8 in a girl or before 9 in a boy, according to the American Academy of Pediatrics.
• In girls: breast development, faster height growth, and possibly early periods.
• In boys: enlargement of the testicles and penis, increased muscle and body hair, faster height growth, and a deeper voice.
• This is usually an early start to normal changes, but sometimes there is a cause needing treatment.
• Body odor or a little pubic or underarm hair may appear before 8 without true puberty; a doctor distinguishes between these.
• Tell the doctor about any cream, medicine or supplement the child uses; some contain hormones that may cause early puberty.

Delayed puberty:
• In boys: no signs by 14; testicular enlargement is the first sign. The most common cause is a normal delay in a healthy boy, often running in the family. He enters puberty with time and usually catches up with peers in height by 18.
• In girls: no signs of puberty by 13, usually starting with breast development, or no periods by 15.
• Possible causes include low weight, excessive exercise, stress, chronic illness or hormone disturbances.

At the doctor's: a calm examination and review of the height chart; the doctor may request hormone blood tests and a hand and wrist X-ray to determine “bone age”. Reassurance and follow-up are often enough. Treatment is usually needed only if the timing causes a physical or psychological problem; the doctor decides.

These are medical timings. The details of the signs of puberty in Islamic law should be sought from scholars.

When to see a doctor: signs before 8 in a girl or before 9 in a boy, no signs by 13 in a girl or 14 in a boy, no periods by 15, or a child who seems much shorter or taller than peers. Reassure the child that the visit is to check that all is well, not because there is something wrong with them.
